catalog_quote: Every written consonant and vowel is pronounced. When consonants are doubled, both are pronounced, as in Italian. The “x” is pronounced like “ch” in [...] “Bach.” The “ṭ” stands for a “t” sound made with the tip of the tongue up in the roof of the mouth. Stress is on the first syllable unless otherwise marked. The vowels are pronounced as follows: [...] u is like the “oo” in “moon.” Awaswas Word List Forms from Curtin are coded “C,” from Henshaw, “H” and from Pinart, “P.”

new_statements.relation_note: Pronunciation guide: all letters pronounced, geminates double, x = [x], dotted t = retroflex, default initial stress with exceptions marked, five-vowel key; then coded word list.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Shipley's normalized Awaswas word list, stress falls on the first syllable by default; words with stress elsewhere carry an explicit mark. A reading convention for the compiled list (c. 700 words from Pinart 1878, Curtin 1884, Henshaw 1888), i.e. Shipley's philological judgement that initial stress is the unmarked case, not a rule from fieldwork.

new_statements.identity_note: Chapter titled 'The Awaswas Language' about the Mission Santa Cruz language; its word list is compiled from Curtin (C), Henshaw (H) and Pinart (P), i.e. the Santa Cruz Costanoan records that define sant1428. Caveat from earlier reading: Pinart's Santa Cruz lists mix in some San Juan Bautista (Mutsun) words. | Santa Cruz Costanoan (= Awaswas) is one of the six Costanoan dialects in the authors' comparative material (abbreviation CR, p. 56; forms such as CR tcare-s 'man'); the accent statement is made for Costanoan as a whole, i.e. group-level statement covering the sampled dialects [name in source: Santa Cruz (Costanoan dialect 'CR'); statement worded for 'Costanoan'; pages 56 (dialect abbreviations), 84-89 ('Accent'), esp. 88-89]

new_statements.quote: In Costanoan, stems of two syllables prevail. But antepenultimate accent occurs, most formative, locative, and modo-temporal suffixes being added to the root without causing a shift of accent. In fact, there is no certain case of any Costanoan word being accented other than on the first syllable of its stem.

sources.note: No rule stated. Henshaw's Santa Cruz (Awaswas) list, recorded 26-29 Sept 1888 (p. 89), is printed as the 'Santa Cruz' column of the Costanoan table pp. [160] ff; the Phonetic Key (unnumbered page before the vocabularies, p. 12) says 'The accented syllable of every word marked by an acute accent.. [In the original, the acute accent marking the syllabic stress is placed sometimes over the letter and sometimes at the end of the syllable.]' So the volume contains per-word stress marks (e.g. u-li' 'head', ha'-kas 'throat', ra-na'-i 'neck', a-la'-cu 'infant', kor'-o 'foot') but no analysis or state…
